latest_articles.title: From exception to norm: Multilingual publics in North Africa and lessons for the theory of the public sphere
latest_articles.abstract: Most societies and polities worldwide are multilingual, yet most theories of public spheres overlook this fact, as they stem from Western contexts dominated by a single national language. Reviewing the scientific literature, I show that multilingualism is often treated as a problem or exception rather than the norm. Drawing on four observations from publics in North Africa, I highlight insights relevant to general theories of public spheres: (1) the role of translation and coexistence of multiple languages within one public sphere; (2) the complex relationship between freedom of speech and language; (3) the correlation between language and levels of critique; and (4) the strategic potential of multilingualism. All point to the ambiguous role of language for publics. Finally, I propose a first draft of a theoretical framework for public spheres that recognizes multilingual realities, showing that existing theories contain elements that can integrate this global condition.
affiliations: Institute for Political and Administrative Sciences, University of Rostock, Rostock, Germany

latest_articles.title: From theatrical exclusivity to platform immediacy: Changing windowing strategies in U.S. cinema
latest_articles.abstract: The sequencing of release windows has traditionally structured film distribution around theatrical exclusivity. In recent decades, however, the rise of digital platforms has challenged this temporal logic, prioritizing immediacy over delay. This article examines how windowing strategies in U.S. cinema have changed between 1990 and 2023, focusing on the progressive reconfiguration of the time intervals separating theatrical, physical, digital, and television releases. Drawing on a longitudinal analysis of the top grossing U.S. films, the study identifies a sustained contraction of release windows, culminating in near-simultaneous, platform-oriented distribution during the 2020s. Rather than treating windowing as a purely economic optimization problem, the article conceptualizes it as a shifting temporal regime shaped by platformization, changing consumption practices, and industrial coordination. By tracing the transition from theatrical exclusivity to platform immediacy, the study contributes to ongoing debates on convergence, distribution, and the transformation of cinematic circulation in the digital era.

latest_articles.title: From Communication Anxiety to Psychological Reliance
latest_articles.abstract: Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study investigates how communication anxiety and psychological need satisfaction relate to the use of Large Language Model (LLM)-based chatbots, specifically ChatGPT, for communication tasks (e.g., writing emails, drafting messages, and preparing scripts). Using a three-wave panel survey of participants from the United States and South Korea, we examined both between- and within-person dynamics. Results showed that individuals with higher trait-level communication anxiety tended to use ChatGPT more frequently for communication tasks, whereas within-person fluctuations in anxiety did not predict greater use. ChatGPT use was positively associated with the satisfaction of basic psychological needs – autonomy, competence, and relatedness – and this need satisfaction, in turn, was associated with greater psychological reliance on ChatGPT. Importantly, need satisfaction further mediated the relationship between ChatGPT use and psychological reliance at both within- and between-person levels. Cultural comparisons revealed that US participants exhibited stronger momentary effects, while Korean participants showed more stable, trait-based patterns. These findings highlight the role of LLM-based chatbots as need-supportive communication tools that may become integrated into users’ communication practices over time, with implications for theories of AI-mediated communication, cross-cultural research, and the design of human-AI communication systems.
affiliations: Department of Media, Kyung Hee University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
Brian Lamb School of Communication, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA
Library, University of California Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA
Department of Communication, University of Illinois Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA

latest_articles.title: Testing the Parasocial Contact Hypothesis Through Stand-Up Comedy
latest_articles.abstract: The study examined how humorous parasocial contact can reduce prejudice toward outgroups. Study predictions were tested in an experiment ( N = 301) comparing the effects of a comedy stand-up by a Muslim comedian (Hasan Minhaj or Mohammed Amer) to a control condition a stand-up from a non-Muslim comedian (Brian Regan or Jim Gaffigan). Results indicated that humorous parasocial contact was effective at facilitating parasocial relationships in all conditions. Consistent with study predictions, when participants were exposed to the mediated intergroup contact with a Muslim comedian, parasocial relationships – mediated through intergroup anxiety – were positively associated with willingness for contacts with Muslims (i.e., negatively associated with social distance) and negatively associated with endorsement of Muslim stereotypes. In contrast, these mediational relationships were not observed when mediated intergroup contact occurred with a White comedian. These and other results are discussed along with implications, limitations, and future research directions.
affiliations: Department of Communication, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA
Department of Communication Studies, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA
Department of Communication Studies, Baruch University, New York, NY, USA

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Helping Insecurely Attached People Regulate Negative Emotions: The Moderating Role of Romantic Partners’ Support on the Effect of Attachment on Appraisal and Eating
latest_articles.abstract: Insecurely attached people have difficulties regulating their emotions and are less likely to use adaptive emotion regulation strategies, such as cognitive reappraisal. Yet, romantic partners may play a pivotal role in helping insecurely attached people reappraise situations and reduce negative emotions. Anxiously and avoidantly attached people, however, may need different types of support to regulate their negative emotions. Some prior research has examined the types of support that are more effective for anxiously and avoidantly attached people, but no work has related attachment orientations and emotion regulation patterns to eating behavior. To address this gap, we conducted a 14-day daily diary study examining these associations to determine: (a) the degree to which anxiously and avoidantly attached people perceived specific types of support from their romantic partner as more effective in regulating their daily negative emotions, and (b) how these perceptions were associated with their daily eating behavior. We found that highly anxious people reported less use of cognitive reappraisal than less anxious people, but that attachment avoidance was not associated with reappraisal. Both attachment anxiety and avoidance, however, were associated with greater negative affect, and the use of reappraisal was associated with less negative affect. Specifically, on days when reappraisal was high, negative affect was more likely to be low compared to days when reappraisal was low. Also, on days when the amount of general support received was high, reappraisal and positive mood after receiving support were also high compared to days when general support received was low. Although eating was not associated with perceived support, it was negatively associated with stress and negative affect. Thus, while matches of partner support type with attachment insecurity did not interact to predict reappraisal, general support received from a partner was associated with greater reappraisal.
affiliations: Department of Community Health and Health Behavior, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA
Department of Psychology, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA

latest_articles.title: Can solutions journalism counter news avoidance? A choice experiment examining effects on emotions, self-efficacy, and news engagement
latest_articles.abstract: Solutions journalism has been proposed as a potential remedy to the negativity bias in news coverage, which is often blamed for emotional exhaustion and disengagement among audiences, eventually leading to news avoidance. However, it remains unclear who is drawn to such content and what effects it produces. This study presents a large-scale choice experiment ( N = 4622) examining preferences for solution-focused versus problem-focused journalism on antibiotic resistance, and the effects on emotions, self-efficacy, and news engagement. Participants were presented with one of four news stories focused on either problems or solutions at either an individual level or societal level. Some participants were assigned to watch a specific news story, and others were free to choose themselves. The results show a clear preference for solutions journalism, particularly when stories are framed at the individual level, though not more strongly among news avoiders. Exposure to solutions journalism increases positive emotions, reduces negative ones, and enhances self-efficacy, but does not boost news engagement (e.g., sharing, searching, or discussion). Together, the findings suggest that solutions journalism can to some extent counter news avoidance, yet it is not a definitive remedy.
affiliations: Centre for Journalism, University of Southern Denmark
School of Social Sciences, Södertörn University

latest_articles.title: Contesting unity: Media representations of national identity in Malaysia’s multilingual press
latest_articles.abstract: This study examined how four selected Malaysian news outlets represented national identity in a multicultural and politically contested society. Drawing on framing theory and Ariely’s (2019) conceptualization of national identity, it analyzed 104 articles published in 2024 by Harian Metro (Malay), Sin Chew Daily (Chinese), The Star (English), and the English-language edition of the digital-native outlet Malaysiakini . The content analysis examined reporting volume, article types, news sources, frames, and tones. Sin Chew contributed the most coverage, while political actors were the dominant sources across all four outlets. “Interethnic harmony, multiculturalism, and diversity” constituted the dominant frame across most outlets, but ethnic tensions and competing interpretations of nationhood persisted. Other frames included the “defense of Malay identity”, “racism against non-Malays”, and “East Malaysia’s marginalization”. Coverage in Harian Metro and The Star was predominantly inclusive, whereas Malaysiakini gave comparatively greater visibility to contestation and democratic deliberation. The findings show that the coverage represented Malaysian national identity as a dynamic and continuously negotiated process. The observed patterns are consistent with differences in the outlets’ linguistic audiences and institutional positions and can be interpreted within the context of Malaysia’s nation-building legacies. The study contributes to framing research by documenting systematic variation across selected legacy and digital-native outlets within the same multilingual media environment.

latest_articles.title: Normative ideals and empirical realities: Viewpoint diversity in the discourse on German arms deliveries to Ukraine
latest_articles.abstract: Criticism of media coverage is an essential democratic mechanism to hold journalism accountable, yet it can also foster distrust and perceptions of media bias. This study examines such tensions through the case of the German media discourse on arms deliveries to Ukraine. Using accusations of one-sided reporting as a starting point, we theorize normative expectations of media diversity in war-related policy discourse and empirically assess how leading German news outlets represented competing viewpoints. Drawing on a two-year corpus (2022-2023) from 14 Leitmedien and employing a hierarchical supervised machine-learning approach based on (large) language models, we classify stances and frames to compute standard diversity indices. The results reveal a balanced distribution of supportive and opposing stances, yet a low diversity of argumentative frames. This pattern suggests that German media exhibited a liberal-aggregative model of diversity, emphasizing coexistence of opinions over deliberative engagement with competing interpretations. Despite frequent claims of uniform pro-government bias, our findings indicate that coverage was more heterogeneous than critics claimed. However, they also point to limited argumentative depth and a tendency to reproduce existing political logics. We discuss the methodological and normative challenges of quantifying diversity, particularly under conditions of war and uncertainty, and argue that criticism of media bias often reflects broader transformations in the perception of journalistic diversity.
affiliations: Leibniz Institute for Media Research/Hans Bredow Institute (HBI), Hamburg, Germany

latest_articles.title: One election, multiple stories: Polarized visual framing and media bias in the 2024 Turkish Mayoral elections
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines visual framing and media bias during Türkiye’s 2024 mayoral elections, a pivotal contest that marked the ruling AKP’s most significant electoral defeat in two decades. It investigates whether patterns of polarization identified in textual coverage extend to visual framing within a highly polarized media system operating under a competitive authoritarian regime. The analysis draws on a dataset of 6926 visuals published during the official campaign period on the websites of 11 legacy and alternative news outlets, covering six major mayoral candidates in İstanbul, Ankara, and İzmir. Using systematic content analysis, the study codes Grabe and Bucy’s visual character framing, and determines disparities in candidate portrayal and visibility across outlets with different political orientations. The findings reveal pronounced asymmetries between pro-government and pro-opposition media in both tone and volume of coverage. Pro-government outlets grant ruling-party candidates greater visibility and more favorable portrayals, while opposition candidates receive comparatively limited or strategically unfavorable framing. These results demonstrate that visual bias operates not only through framing choices but also through systematic exposure inequalities. The study argues that visual framing reinforces polarization and ruling-party advantage, contributing to the reproduction of uneven political competition in competitive authoritarian regimes.

latest_articles.title: Gendered algorithms within the politics of inclusion in Chinese gaming: a feminist critique of Identity V
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how gender inclusion and inequality coexist in Identity V, a Chinese asymmetrical survival-horror game promoted as gender-inclusive. Combining critical play analysis, participant observation, and eighteen interviews with ten women working across China’s game industry, I trace gender across gameplay, player communities, and production. I argue that avatar design, ranking and matchmaking, monetization, and moderation reproduce masculine-coded forms of competition while positioning women unevenly as players, consumers, and creators. These patterns emerge within workplace hierarchies, market pressures, and state regulation shaped by the intertwined legacies of colonialism, state socialism, market reform, and nationalist gender politics. Yet women also negotiate these constraints through collective practices: players share strategies against harassment, build support networks, and reinterpret gender-conscious design, while practitioners exchange knowledge, refer one another to jobs, mentor newcomers, and make leadership more imaginable. Combining feminist game studies, critical information studies, and feminist ethics of care, the article treats algorithms as sociotechnical infrastructures rather than neutral code. It advances a situated feminist critique of Chinese gaming that moves beyond representation to ask who designs, maintains, and reshapes the systems that govern play.

latest_articles.title: Color evasion, white normativity and ethnic-racial socialization in Chinese-Dutch families
latest_articles.abstract: Critical Race Theory problematizes color evasion and White normativity as phenomena that perpetuate racial injustice, but there is little research on these issues outside the U.S. or with underrepresented ethnic-racial groups. This study examines to what extent Chinese-Dutch mothers ( N = 78) based in the Netherlands show color evasion and White normativity when observed in a social categorization game with their children (ages 7–11 years), as well as self-reported ethnic-racial socialization practices. Mothers showed color evasion by avoiding ethnic-racial questions even though these were crucial to game efficiency, and mothers asked such questions later and took more time to formulate them. White normativity was also present as mothers were more likely to reference the Black and Asian targets than the White targets, who appear to be seen as the norm from which the others deviate. These behaviors were unrelated to mothers’ self-reported ethnic-racial socialization practices. These results suggest that Chinese-Dutch children are exposed to racialized social norms that are associated with prejudice against marginalized ethnic-racial groups, including their own. The findings are discussed in terms of implicit and explicit ethnic-racial socialization and their causes and consequences.

latest_articles.title: Friendship as emotional infrastructure: Sustaining belonging and educational participation among racialised young women in Spain
latest_articles.abstract: Educational inclusion is often discussed in terms of access, attainment, institutional barriers, and unequal outcomes. However, for racialised young women, educational trajectories are also shaped by the everyday relationships through which belonging, recognition, safety, and exclusion are experienced. Friendship is one of these relationships, yet it is often treated as secondary to formal schooling or analysed mainly through peer effects, social capital, support, or interethnic contact. This article explores how friendships shape the educational trajectories of racialised young women in Spain and how they may sustain belonging and participation across unequal educational contexts. Drawing on 65 semi-structured interviews with women aged 18-29 from Roma, Latin American, North and Sub-Saharan African, South Asian, and broader Asian backgrounds, conducted within the #FriendsMatter research project, the study identifies friendship as an emotional infrastructure in educational life. The findings show that compulsory schooling was frequently experienced through peer racism, limited intercultural engagement, and institutional misrecognition, which constrained the formation of emotionally sustaining friendships. In post-compulsory education, however, friendships often created spaces of emotional safety, enabled recognition and relational legitimacy, and provided continuity across educational transitions. The article argues that friendships matter educationally not merely because they provide support, but because they can stabilise belonging and participation over time. In doing so, it contributes to debates on educational inclusion, recognition, and belonging by showing that friendship is a constitutive dimension of educational participation itself.

latest_articles.title: From global citizenship to inclusive classroom practices: Parallel mediation by cultural intelligence and multicultural empathy
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigated the relationships between global citizenship, cultural intelligence, multicultural empathic tendency, and inclusive classroom practices among primary school teachers working in Diyarbakır. Data were collected using scales targeting the relevant variables in this cross-sectional survey; the measurement model was re-evaluated through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and reliability/validity evidence. Inter-structure relationships were tested within the framework of a structural equation model established using a parallel mediation approach, and indirect associations were examined using a bootstrap-based method. The findings suggest that the relationship between global citizenship and inclusive classroom practices was observed indirectly, rather than directly, through cultural intelligence and multicultural empathic tendency. Multicultural empathic tendency showed a more prominent indirect pathway, while cultural intelligence played a more limited but statistically significant and complementary role. The results suggest that cultural-cognitive capacities and socio-affective sensitivity to cultural differences may help explain how global citizenship orientations are associated with inclusive teaching behaviors.

latest_articles.title: Majority adoption dynamics: Planes and domains and the primary role of diversity ideologies
latest_articles.abstract: Acculturation has been conceptualized as a bidirectional process in which both minority and majority groups undergo cultural changes as a result of intergroup contact. However, most studies have focused on the acculturation of minority groups, neglecting the analysis of changes occurring within the majority population. This study examines the acculturation of native Spaniards, specifically their adoption and preference for adoption of cultural elements from people of Moroccan origin. An adapted version of the Relative Acculturation Extended Model (RAEM) was used, distinguishing between real and ideal planes and between peripheral and central life domains. The role of contact quality and diversity ideologies (multiculturalism and intercultural sensitivity) was also analysed. A total of 361 native Spaniards (53.4% women) completed an online questionnaire. Results showed that scores were higher in peripheral than in central domains, and in the ideal than in the real plane, although absolute levels were generally low, especially in central domains. Interaction analyses revealed significant two-way interactions between contact quality and multiculturalism in peripheral domains of the real plane and central domains of the ideal plane. Simple effects indicated that contact quality was positively associated with cultural adoption in peripheral domains at moderate and high levels of multiculturalism, and with preferences for adoption in central domains only at high levels of multiculturalism. These findings expand current understanding of majority acculturation and suggest lower resistance to the adoption of minority cultural elements in peripheral than in central domains, particularly when contact quality is accompanied by multicultural orientations.

latest_articles.title: Navigating emerging adulthood away from home: A structural equation modeling study of psychological, sociocultural, and academic adaptation among international students in Hungary
latest_articles.abstract: The present study examines emerging adulthood ( Arnett, 2000 ) in the context of acculturation among international higher education students in Hungary. Specifically, the aim was to test an integrated structural model examining how developmental, contextual, acculturation-related, and individual factors relate to the psychological, sociocultural, and academic adaptation of international students. Data were collected via an online questionnaire. A total of 859 participants ( M age = 23.84, SD = 2.32) were included in the structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis. The final SEM demonstrated good global and local fit to the data (RMSEA =.052, SRMR =.037, CFI =.977, TLI =.950). The results suggest that, of all the variables studied, instability during emerging adulthood and perception of an international student-friendly university environment were the most important factors in psychological, academic, and sociocultural adaptation. Among the adaptation outcomes, academic adaptation emerged as the most reliably predicted variable, showing the strongest association with perceived university supportiveness. These results indicate that emerging adulthood is, in many respects, a sensitive time window and not merely a transitional stage of life, but also a complex psychosocial period shaped by cultural, social, and institutional factors. For students studying abroad, acculturation and the developmental transitions of young adulthood appear to interact dynamically. Overall, the study highlights the importance of developmentally and culturally sensitive mental health support for international students during this transitional life stage.

latest_articles.title: Support for indigenous and multicultural rights and intergroup attitudes in New Zealand: The role of indispensability
latest_articles.abstract: Different ethnic groups can be considered more positively if they are perceived to be indispensable for society, either in terms of ‘who we are’ -identity indispensability- or ‘what we do’- functional indispensability. In this study we expand the boundaries of indispensability research by investigating the role of perceived indispensability of Indigenous (Māori) and immigrant (Chinese) groups on intergroup outcomes (support for rights and outgroup attitudes) in New Zealand, a settler colonial society. We also considered the role of perceived diversity ideologies of interculturalism (identity-conscious) and colorblindness (identity-blind) on these intergroup outcomes. Given New Zealand’s bicultural history, we expected Māori to be rated higher on identity indispensability but lower on functional indispensability than Chinese New Zealanders. In this study, 174 New Zealand university students of European descent (Pākehā), with a mean age of 19.1 years, answered the online survey. As expected, participants rated Māori higher on identity indispensability but lower on functional indispensability than Chinese New Zealanders. Perceived identity indispensability of Māori was the strongest significant predictor of support for Māori rights. Perceived functional indispensability of Chinese New Zealanders positively predicted support for multicultural rights and outgroup attitudes. Perceived interculturalism was positively associated with support for multicultural rights and attitudes toward Chinese New Zealanders. The results are discussed in terms of the promising role of perceived indispensability of both Indigenous and migrant groups for more harmonious and equitable societies.

latest_articles.title: Values, flourishing, and identity integration: Understanding alcohol and other drug use among African Australian youth
latest_articles.abstract: Previous research suggests Alcohol and Other Drug (AOD) use by sub-Saharan African (SSA) youth who emigrate to Western cultural contexts like Australia is an indication of their acculturation and is influenced by their values. Although values are distal predictors of AOD use, the extent to which SSA Australian youth apply their values in AOD use could be a function of their psychological flourishing and Bicultural Identity Integration (BII). The aim of this study was to test a predictive model that combines values, psychological flourishing and BII to explore how the interaction of personal values and adaptive resources are related to AOD use among SSA Australian youth ( N = 196, M age = 23.7 years, range = 16 – 35 years). Participants completed an online questionnaire, and the data was analysed using Structural Equation Modelling. We found that conservation and self-transcendence values, which are conceptualized as collectivistic or social focus values by S. H. Schwartz (2012) negatively predicted alcohol use through the serial mediation effects of psychological flourishing and BII. At the same time, these values negatively predicted other drug use through the serial mediation effects of psychological flourishing and BII, and alcohol use. Self-enhancement (but not openness to change) positively and significantly predicted alcohol use through the serial mediation effects of psychological flourishing and BII. Self-enhancement values also positively predicted other drug use through the serial mediation effects of psychological flourishing and BII, and alcohol use. The findings support the hypothesis that collectivist values negatively predict AOD use among SSA Australian youth through their psychological flourishing and BII. The results are discussed in terms of interventions to reduce AOD-related harm among immigrant youth who are acculturating to new norms and behaviours.

latest_articles.title: “We are outdoor people, but now you find that you are staying indoors for two days.” A qualitative study on perceptions and experiences of African migrant students in China
latest_articles.abstract: Every year, thousands of African students migrate to high- and middle-income countries to pursue higher education. China has emerged as an educational destination for many of them. Understanding the impacts of migration on students is relevant for developing recommendations to support their psychosocial health. This study aims to explore the perceptions and experiences of Southern African migrants studying in China. This was a qualitative study that used semi-structured interviews (n = 20) and one focus group discussion with five participants. Data collection was conducted in English, in person in Nanjing, China, during 2024. Interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed. Coding and thematic analysis was conducted using Quirkos software. Thematic analysis identified three overarching categories, motivation to migrate, barriers as cumulative losses, and facilitators. Barriers included 1) language and communication, 2) cultural displacement and disruption of everyday practices, 3) economic constraints, 4) social isolation and relational loss, 5) racial discrimination, and 6) psychosocial impact as expression of migratory grief. Alongside facilitators such as 1) peer networks, 2) engaging in hobbies, 3) transnational ties and emotional support, and 4) safety. This study highlights the experiences of African students in China, characterized by challenges related to isolation, language barriers, cultural gaps, and financial stress, all of which affect their psychosocial health. Facilitators included learning Chinese, peer-support networks, establishing good relationships with their supervisors and/or colleagues, keeping close contact with their families and friends, and engaging in hobbies. Participants recommended institutions and governments to include measures for social integration, financial support opportunities, offering language courses, and ensuring access to peer-led initiatives and counselling. While students reported coping strategies, targeted strategies such as inclusive social events, Chinese language courses, and cultural orientation programs, could foster integration, support mental health, and optimize learning. Addressing these barriers and strengthening existing facilitators would enable institutions to create more supportive environments that promote academic success, wellbeing, and social connectivity for African students in China.

latest_articles.title: Negotiated autonomy: A typology of negotiation strategies in podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism in Turkey
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts negotiate neoliberal entrepreneurial demands within a precarious, platform-based media environment. Existing scholarship has conceptualized journalists’ responses to precarious and neoliberal labor conditions through concepts such as resistance, coping, and resilience. This study proposes negotiation as a distinct strategic response that captures how journalists selectively recalibrate the terms and boundaries of their engagement with structural demands through conditional acceptance, refusal, modification, and boundary-setting. The study is based on in-depth interviews with 10 entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts in Türkiye, with the interview data analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings identify four interrelated negotiation strategies embedded in the everyday production practices of podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism: ethical negotiation, temporal negotiation, visibility negotiation, and collective negotiation. These strategies respond respectively to neoliberal pressures associated with commercialization, continuous productivity, personal branding, and the individualization of labor; however, they remain constrained by financial precarity, platform visibility pressures, and fragile conditions of sustainability. The findings show that entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts selectively recalibrate the terms and boundaries of their engagement with neoliberal demands while remaining embedded within structural constraints and preserving limited spaces of professional autonomy. By conceptualizing negotiation as a distinct form of strategic response and identifying its four empirical forms, the study contributes a typology for explaining how bounded and provisional professional autonomy is produced under persistent structural constraints in podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism.

latest_articles.title: Prioritizing Journalistic Norms or Humanitarian Values? A Multistage Computational Analysis of Journalistic Role Performance in Humanitarian News
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how journalistic roles are performed in humanitarian news. Using a multistage computational approach applied to news data from 46 international news organizations across 21 countries, we find that role performance varies systematically across topics, political systems, and organizational types. Our findings complicate the predominant tendency in humanitarian journalism scholarship to frame roles in terms of professional norms or humanitarian values. Instead, we show that role performance is multidimensional and contextually contingent. Improving humanitarian coverage therefore requires attention not only to professional practices but also to the institutional conditions that enable diverse forms of journalism.
affiliations: University of East Anglia, Norwich, UK

latest_articles.title: Bridging worlds: Language, translation and missionary accommodation in Yuan China (13th–14th centuries)
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines linguistic mediation and missionary accommodation in Yuan China during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, situating evidence from Yuan territory within the wider multilingual context of the Mongol world. Drawing on missionary letters, travel narratives, papal documents and Chinese administrative sources, it analyses how access to languages, interpreters, translation and teaching shaped missionaries’ capacity to communicate and exercise religious authority. Particular attention is given to the contrasting experiences of William of Rubruck and Giovanni da Montecorvino. While Rubruck’s dependence on interpreters reveals the constraints imposed by limited linguistic access, Montecorvino’s reported competence in Mongolian enabled translation, reading and preaching, although the surviving evidence does not permit reconstruction of his language-learning methods. His simultaneous translation of Christian texts into Mongolian and teaching of Greek and Latin further shows that missionary accommodation combined adaptation with the transmission of European linguistic practices. Yuan administrative sources provide a complementary perspective by showing how Christianity was incorporated into imperial structures of religious governance. The article argues that linguistic mediation was constitutive of missionary activity because access to linguistic resources shaped the distribution of communicative agency and, consequently, the conditions under which religious authority could be exercised. • Investigates missionary linguistic accommodation in Yuan China. • Analyses translation and interpreting in cross-cultural encounters. • Examines multilingual communication in the Mongol Empire. • Draws on European and Chinese historical sources. • Reframes missionary activity through the lens of language mediation.

latest_articles.title: Taking an Agnostic Stance: The Use of “I Don't Know”-Questions in Dutch Home Visits about Child Vaccination
latest_articles.abstract: In healthcare encounters, questions play a fundamental role. Through their design, questions impose constraints on answers and convey how strictly these constraints should be adhered to. Using Conversation Analysis, we investigate one mechanism through which such constraints are regulated in question-answer sequences in Dutch home visits: “ I don't know ”-questions (IDK-questions). We demonstrate that, in using this format, speakers adopt an agnostic stance towards what follows in their questions, thus lowering the constraints imposed on recipients' answers. This allows for responses that could otherwise be construed as misaligned, dispreferred, or identity-threatening. Thus, IDK-questions constitute a useful practice for forestalling interactional tension, for promoting progressivity, and for preserving social solidarity, especially in environments where the delicate matter of child vaccination is discussed.

latest_articles.title: Talking to and for whom?: Orienting to the audience in Indonesian broadcast interviews
latest_articles.abstract: As a genre of institutional talk, broadcast interviews require interviewers and interviewees to design their talk for an overhearing audience. Based on data from Indonesian broadcast interviews, this study explores the tension that arises between adhering to this institutional norm and simultaneously addressing one another. Focusing on references to person deployed within a story told by an interviewee depicting two figures in conflict, the analysis demonstrates how both co-participants and the audience construe the storytelling as a departure from this norm. Co-participants' responses to the telling—including laughter, gaze aversion, elaborate postural shifts, participation in story reenactments and engagement in mutual blame—suggest that they treat the responsibility for maintaining the norm as a matter of mutual accountability rather than one attributable solely to interviewers, who are institutionally tasked with managing the interview process.

latest_articles.title: Ambivalence and antagonism: The intertwinement of gossiping and public shaming on social media
latest_articles.abstract: The vernacular practices of public shaming and gossiping on social media function both as entertainment and as disciplinary mechanisms. This article investigates two Finnish subreddits on Reddit, where gossiping and public shaming practices are closely intertwined. On these subreddits, screenshots of Finnish social media content creators’ posts are intensely circulated, scrutinised and dissected. This article examines how the gossiping practices are tied to the vernacular practices of public shaming on social media and what these practices are affixed to within the discourses created on these subreddits. The study found that the entertainment and judgement derived from these practices are tethered to themes of unpredictability, ambivalence and community building. These create moral discourses about non-normative ways of self-presentation and public conduct, both in corporal and online realms. Moreover, this study exemplifies that when gossiping and public shaming on social media intertwine, the line between disciplining and bullying becomes easier to cross.

latest_articles.title: Fuck You, Pay Me: Payment apps, review platforms, and ambivalent resistance in the influencer industry
latest_articles.abstract: This article critically examines emerging intermediaries in the influencer industry that aggregate anonymous reviews of brands and allow influencers to report how much they were paid. Turning to four intermediaries (Fuck You Pay Me, Willa, Hashtag Pay Me, and Clara for Creators), I argue that although these emerging intermediaries represent an important step toward creating more equity, these efforts are a double-edged sword and represent a form of ambivalent resistance to broader structures governing the influencer industry. While these intermediaries are used to resist the precarity of platformized and branded cultural production, these transactions have the potential to be co-opted—used for surveillance and data tracking by brands, platforms, and corporations—potentially blunting emerging forms of collective action and solidarity. Ultimately, these intermediaries provide an opportunity to theorize forms of resistance to precarity as neither “top-down” nor “bottom-up,” but rather a means of negotiating and navigating power from limited and precarious positions.

latest_articles.title: Paid, but not a partner: Monetization without standing in Facebook’s Performance Bonus Program
latest_articles.abstract: Platform revenue-sharing programs both pay and govern creators. Drawing on interviews with 18 participants in Facebook’s Performance Bonus Program (PBP) and the author’s own participation, this study examines how monetization reshaped creators’ platform governance expectations. PBP’s onboarding, which addressed recipients as “valued creators” and promised earnings of “up to $30,000 a month,” combined with early recurring payouts to cultivate expectations of continuity and institutional responsiveness, particularly among participants new to monetization. When enforcement errors, payout volatility, and support failures followed, participants discovered that payment had not conferred meaningful access to explanation, human review, or recourse. This article theorizes that condition as monetization without standing : a governance arrangement in which creators are compensated and governed as laborers while denied the procedural recognition typically associated with paid work. This arrangement constitutes a breach of the psychological contract generated by monetization, producing durable behavioral constraint, disparate impacts on marginalized creators, and creator attrition.

latest_articles.title: Agency, artificial intelligence, and the non-anthropocentric turn in public relations
latest_articles.abstract: This paper argues that the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly Generative AI (GenAI), necessitates a fundamental reorientation of public relations (PR) scholarship beyond its anthropocentric foundational assumptions. Traditionally, anthropocentrism positions agency as an exclusively human capacity and clings to the inherited dualisms of ‘modern’ thinking. Yet more-than-human entities, including GenAI actors, become active agents, co-constituting a world where nature, humans, and technologies are deeply entangled. They always were, but now this entanglement is increasingly difficult to ignore. We propose that scholars engage with a non-anthropocentric (post-human) turn in PR. One way, which we adopt, of beginning this reflection is by synthesising Actor-Network Theory (ANT) and the notion of symbiotic agency to (re)conceptualise agency as a relational, hybrid process that emerges through interactions among human (e.g., PR practitioners) and more-than-human actors (e.g. GenAI). This approach advances a refreshed, dynamic understanding of PR enacted by a variety of actors, disrupting the human-technology dichotomy and recognising AI as an active participant in a shared network or ecology. It also extends power in PR as post-hegemonic, arising from material interactions rather than solely representational discourse.

latest_articles.title: Agonistic engagement: An architecture for participation
latest_articles.abstract: Engagement is widely promoted in public relations as a response to complex and contested social issues, yet it is often operationalized in ways that remain organization-centred, consensus-oriented, and inattentive to power and disagreement. This paper contributes an agonistic co-design architecture for operationalizing engagement through staged participatory tools. Drawing on agonistic democratic theory, design thinking, and participatory co-design, the model conceptualizes engagement as a designed process that accommodates dissensus rather than suppressing it. The architecture maps engagement across four iterative stages—discover, define, develop, and deliver—and offers a typology of participatory tools aligned to each stage. Three evaluative dimensions—participation potential, agonistic capacity, and social value—are introduced to support systematic assessment of how engagement designs enable influence, manage disagreement, and generate outcomes beyond organizational benefit. Positioned as a conceptual design framework, the model provides a theoretically grounded and practically actionable architecture for analyzing, designing, and evaluating participatory engagement in contested contexts.

latest_articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and the paradox of the positive
latest_articles.abstract: As AI becomes more ubiquitous and entrenched in our everyday world, students, communication professionals, and researchers are increasingly turning to, or being pushed to use, AI for research, writing, or simply for companionship. While AI is widely framed as enhancing productivity and efficiency, emerging evidence increasingly challenges these claims. Drawing on the paradox of the positive, the hype cycle, and related critical frameworks, this study examines how optimistic narratives surrounding AI obscure its limitations, risks, and structural harms. Through a critical analysis of public relations scholarship, alongside mainstream media coverage of AI, the study explores systemic concerns such as hallucination, misinformation, the erosion of cognitive and professional skills, labor exploitation, environmental costs, and ethical failures rooted in opaque and extractive data practices. The analysis reveals a disconnect between critical stakeholder concerns and the optimistic assumptions reflected in public relations literature and practice that AI supports organization–public relationships or that AI-related risks can be effectively addressed. The article argues that current manifestations of AI often undermine learning, professional judgment, and public trust, and offers recommendations for a more critical and cautious approach to AI use by scholars, educators, and communication professionals.

latest_articles.title: Can AI-assisted apologies foster trust and forgiveness? The role of warmth and competence in crisis communication tone
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how perceived authorship and relational tone jointly influence audience responses to AI-assisted crisis apologies. Using a 4 (perceived authorship: AI, human, mixed, control) × 2 (relational tone: competence, warmth) factorial design, we investigate whether warmth-focused language can moderate the relationship between AI authorship and perceived sincerity, which in turn influences audience responses to crisis apologies. Results show that apologies perceived as human-authored are evaluated as more sincere, leading to higher trust and forgiveness intentions. In contrast, apologies perceived as AI-authored increase machine heuristic perceptions, which lower perceived sincerity, and subsequently, trust and forgiveness intentions. Warmth moderates the relationship between perceived authorship and sincerity for apologies perceived as human-authored but fails to attenuate the negative indirect effects of machine heuristic processing for apologies perceived as AI-authored. We ground this asymmetric pattern in need for cognitive closure theory, arguing that an unambiguous AI authorship cue triggers cognitive closure on the communicator’s nature, rendering subsequent warmth-focused cues incongruent with the already-formed judgment and therefore discounted. The SCM provides a complementary account of why the AI stereotype resists message-level updating while the human category remains open to elaboration. These findings advance theoretical understanding of divergent audience processing in AI-mediated crisis communication and carry practical implications for how organizations deploy AI in high-stakes apology contexts where authenticity is closely scrutinized.

latest_articles.title: Crisis management in South Asia: Toward a care-centered government crisis communication framework
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines government crisis communication and media framing of the Bangladesh Air Force jet crash. Guided by Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT), framing theory, and ethics of care, we investigated official response strategies and media coverage of the crisis event. We employed a mixed-methods design that combined thematic analysis of government press releases with computational analysis of 544 news articles. Findings showed that government communication reflected SCCT-consistent strategies, including instructing and adjusting information, corrective action, transparency about systemic weaknesses, and bolstering through heroism and solidarity. Media coverage extended the crisis narrative beyond incident reporting by foregrounding human suffering and public accountability. The analysis also showed that care was communicated through ritualized mourning, victim-centered support, emotional listening, and moral recognition of sacrifice. Based on these findings, we propose a preliminary Care-Centered Government Crisis Communication Framework , showing how meaning-making and crisis legitimacy in state-involved aviation disasters are co-constructed through procedural responsiveness, moral recognition, and media-mediated accountability. The study contributes to crisis communication and government public relations scholarship by centering care, accountability, and cultural context in public-sector crisis response in South Asia.

latest_articles.title: Crushing identity spices into Chutney: Blending personal, professional, and social identities in DEI communication for stakeholder identification
latest_articles.abstract: This conceptual essay advances critical public relations scholarship by introducing the identity chutney framework as a multidimensional, intersectional approach to organizational diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) communication. This essay argues that organizational DEI discourse privileges demographic markers of identity such as ethnicity and gender while marginalizing personal and professional dimensions. This reductive framing risks misaligning organizational DEI communication with the lived realities of stakeholders whose identities are increasingly fluid and complex. In response, the identity chutney framework conceptualizes identity as integrated. Drawing on theories of identity, signaling, and stakeholder identification, the framework proposes that effective organizational DEI communication should blend dimensions of personal identity (such as personality traits and interests), social identity (such as gender and ethnicity), and professional identity (such as skills and expertise). Like chutney , its value lies not in any single component but in the richness created through their integration. By emphasizing authentic storytelling, purpose-driven messaging, and the alignment of visual and narrative cues, the identity chutney framework advances existing DEI communication approaches by better reflecting the complexities of intersectionality across multiple identity dimensions. The identity chutney framework contributes to critical public relations that reframes public relations as a practice accountable to humanity and attentive to inequality, by offering a more nuanced lens that advances social justice by foregrounding the heterogeneity of lived experiences, obscured by mass categorizations of the marginalized.

latest_articles.title: Effects of channels and decision justifications on perceptions of organizational listening
latest_articles.abstract: Extensive research on organizational listening has provided some general guidelines on how organizational listening should be conducted to address stakeholders’ concerns and needs. One of these guidelines relates to engaging with stakeholders on listening channels that they already use and incorporating their viewpoints into decision-making. Meanwhile, there is a lack of research that empirically explores how these practices influence perceptions. This study conducted a 3 × 4 experiment with a nationally representative sample of 426 Australian citizens. Using a hypothetical local council’s efforts to listen to its local constituents about the housing issue as an example, this study tested the effects of three channels (i.e., community forum, online form, and Facebook) and four decision justifications (i.e., consensus, majority view, strategic alignment, and further consultation) on the dynamics of trust and perceptions of selective listening, inclusive listening, and self-orientation. For listening channels, community forum was rated the highest for trust and Facebook was rated the lowest. For decision justifications, consensus and majority both increased trust but strategic alignment reduced trust. Furthermore, the models tested showed that trust enhanced perceptions of inclusive listening, which was critical for reducing perceptions of self-orientation. The findings demonstrated that in addition to how to conduct the organizational listening process, it is also crucial to consider factors that influence perceptions during the process. (198 words)

latest_articles.title: Engaging Muslims through dialogic ESG communication in the Middle East and North Africa
latest_articles.abstract: This study introduces a dialogic, Islamically sensitive conceptual framework and corresponding scale for ESG communication, based on two waves of online surveys in the MENA region, where Islam is the predominant religion. It shifts from traditional one-way reporting to a dialogic and culturally sensitive approach. The findings reveal that Muslim participants shared expectations that multinationals’ ESG communication should cover environmental sustainability, align with Islamic business ethics, and involve dialogic communication. The study also identifies preferred communication sources, channels, and content formats for Muslims, highlighting differences between frequent stock traders and non-traders. The scale was validated by assessing its relationship with ESG knowledge and corporate reputation.

latest_articles.title: Grand strategy and reputational security: Evaluating the strategic narratives of Global Ireland 2025
latest_articles.abstract: Governments implement public diplomacy campaigns to manage foreign perceptions and build reputational security. We examine Global Ireland 2025 as a case of grand strategy in political public relations, designed to repair the reputational damage of Ireland’s 2008–2018 economic collapse and financial crisis. Focusing on organizational storytelling, we use a discourse analysis to identify and map the strategic narratives the government employed to cultivate perceptions of a stronger, more secure Ireland. Based on policy documents, the Irish government adopted a cooperative grand strategy, emphasizing identity narratives of global citizenship, system narratives of interdependence, and intermestic issue narratives speaking both to domestic and foreign publics. This reinforced Ireland’s cultural identity as forged from historical trauma to rebuild the national self-confidence and project that strength abroad to repair the reputational damage inflicted by the European Union’s bailout. This lends a perceived authenticity, legitimacy, and credibility with which Ireland can effectively counter adversarial narratives, persuade skeptics, and mobilize allies in pursuit of its security and prosperity. This expands public relations scholarship by contextualizing public diplomacy as the securitization of reputation management and trauma as a foundation for national identity formation and projection. Further, it informs public relations practice by demonstrating how grand strategy campaigns can be evaluated.

latest_articles.title: How AI induces professional identity threats: A survey study with public relations professionals
latest_articles.abstract: The transformative force of AI is largely redefining how public relations professionals approach their work, understand their responsibilities, and make sense of the meaning and value associated with being a PR practitioner. While research in other disciplines have increasingly recognized the implications of AI toward professional identities, this topic remains underexplored in the public relations field. Through a quantitative survey (N = 285), we assessed how PR practitioners experience professional identity threats across five dimensions: expertise, status position, autonomy, professional influence, and job responsibility. Our findings highlight that these perceived threats are associated with a combination of factors, including AI use patterns, attitudes and assessment of AI, and influences from leaders and peers. Overall, this study contributes to ongoing conversations about the impact of AI toward the future of public relations through a novel perspective exploring PR professional identities. It also offers practical insights for leaders and organizations on strategies to support PR practitioners in successfully navigating the AI-driven public relations landscape.

latest_articles.title: Issues management by purpose-driven organizations: Critical infrastructure electric utilities address COVID-19 and the digital divide
latest_articles.abstract: Critical infrastructure evolves through collaboration between multiple private sector companies and public agencies. Interactions of critical infrastructure utilities with publics entail significant dynamics of legitimacy and power, the central foci of public relations issues management literature. This study highlights nuances in the cocreational issues management between critical infrastructure utilities and their publics. Specific observations include that cultivated networks bolstered legitimacy of information sources, cooperative utilities relied heavily on establishing organizational legitimacy with member/owner publics when communicating about changes resulting from external influences, and that cooperative utilities felt a deep sense of responsibility for and engagement with their communities, which guided organizational policy and service adaptations during the COVID-19 pandemic. This study extends existing issues management literature of critical infrastructure utilities, which are currently under-represented.

latest_articles.title: Living the messiness: Advancing relationship management theory through embodied ethnography
latest_articles.abstract: Relationship management theory (RMT) is central to public relations scholarship, yet its dominant models continue to privilege stability, linearity, and dyadic exchange. This paper argues that advancing RMT requires methodological innovation capable of capturing the lived complexity of organizational–public relationship (OPR). Drawing on an embodied ethnography with five translocal organizations in Southwest China, we demonstrate how embodied ethnography functions as a theory-generative method in public relations. By foregrounding long-term bodily immersion, multisensory engagement, and participatory action, the method renders visible relational dynamics that are difficult to access through formalized interviews or short-term qualitative approaches. From these embodied encounters, we develop the concept of the messiness of relationship management , articulated through two interrelated dimensions: flux , which captures the cyclical and unstable movement of relationships over time, and plurality , which highlights the simultaneous involvement of multiple actors, roles, and cultural logics. We argue that embodied ethnography advances public relations theory by repositioning instability and multiplicity as constitutive features of relationship management rather than analytical anomalies.

latest_articles.title: Politics, power, and professional practice: Cultural control in an Indian political public relations department
latest_articles.abstract: This article develops a theoretical framework of professional cultural logics to explain how power is enacted, moralized, and reproduced in political public relations practice in India. Drawing on fifty-six hours of video ethnography and multimodal analysis of workplace interactions during the 2019 Indian General Election, the study examines how everyday communicative routines fuse organizational expectations with historically embedded cultural norms. The analysis shows that professional PR goals such as visibility, narrative control, and message localization intersect with cultural logics of duty, hierarchy, obedience, and moralized authority. Through close examination of spatial arrangements, dress codes, gesture, tone, linguistic registers, and routine managerial interactions, the article demonstrates how seemingly mundane communicative acts materialize symbolic and disciplinary power in ways far more nuanced than envisaged by Western critical theorists. These acts transform PR work into a cultural practice in which obedience, loyalty, and moral obligation become central to professional conduct. Design practices further reproduce these logics by visually affirming organizational hierarchies and cultural ideologies. The framework positions culture not as a background condition but as an infrastructure of power. In doing so, the study advances critical public relations scholarship by reframing professionalism as a culturally situated mode of power.

latest_articles.title: Public relations in the AI ecosystem: Structural invisibility and critical challenges
latest_articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become the central organizational infrastructure of contemporary communication, reconfiguring the forms of visibility, legitimacy, and power within the ecosystem. This article examines how Public Relations (PR) are structurally decentered in this environment because of a process of structural invisibility that disconnects their discursive recognition from their effective access to resources, investment, and capacity for influence. Drawing on critical frameworks from political economy, the theory of symbolic capital and agonistic approaches in PR, the study argues that infrastructures privilege logics of automation, scalability and quantification that collide with the relational, contextual and ethical nature of professional practice.We included a global sample of 4,774 organizations linked to AI is analyzed using machine learning techniques. The results show that PR start-ups associated with AI occupy a systematically peripheral position: lower capitalization, fewer investors, more irregular financial trajectories, and higher labor dependency ratios. Paradoxically, this structural deficit coexists with a relatively high symbolic visibility, particularly in media coverage, a pattern that reveals the gap between symbolic capital and economic capital that defines their marginalization in the AI ecosystem.The article concludes that this invisibilization is not accidental, but rather the product of platformization, financialization and epistemic exclusion logics that determine who can influence the design of AI. It is proposed that PR should respond not by accelerating an uncritical integration, but by adopting strategies of slow implementation, regulatory participation, and the articulation of coalitions with equally marginalized actors in order to contest the values that structure the communicative future.

latest_articles.title: Public relations realities: Materiality and the communicative constitution of organizations, publics, and their relationships
latest_articles.abstract: Dominant approaches to theorizing public relations have focused on how the practice, as a management function, can benefit corporate outcomes that align with neoliberal, capitalist ends. In contrast, critical scholars have sought to resist these notions by acknowledging how public relations can function to reinforce existing power structures and seeking to reimagine public relations as a cocreational space that can promote democratic participation. To continue to advance critical public relations scholarship, in this paper we introduce the communicative constitution of organizations perspective, with a specific conceptual focus on materiality, as a path forward for the discipline to continue to resist neoliberal logics. In turn, we offer three possible scholarly avenues for critical public relations researchers to pursue to advance critical scholarship in the discipline through the application of a constitutive approach to materiality. Specifically, we focus on advancing critical scholarship related to: (1) publics, (2) crisis communication, and (3) advocacy and activism.

latest_articles.title: When do social norms strategies reduce uncertainty and anxiety? The moderating role of psychological distance in crisis communication
latest_articles.abstract: Crises such as pandemics, wars, and environmental disasters disrupt public expectations and heighten uncertainty and anxiety. In these contexts, effective communication strategies are essential for helping individuals cope. Social-norm-based messages are often used to guide behavior and foster collective identity and emotional support, yet their cognitive and emotional impact in crisis communication remains underexplored. This study investigated whether and when social norms reduce uncertainty discrepancy and anxiety, and whether perceived psychological distance moderates these effects. A preregistered online experiment (N = 380) employed a between-subjects design, using the Fukushima nuclear wastewater release as the crisis stimulus. Contrary to expectations, no direct effects of descriptive or injunctive norms on uncertainty discrepancy or anxiety were found, nor did psychological distance moderate these effects. However, the exploratory findings revealed that the presence versus absence of social norms mattered in interaction with psychological distance: social-norm-based messages reduced anxiety among psychologically close individuals, whereas they reduced uncertainty discrepancy among psychologically moderate to distant participants. In addition, higher uncertainty discrepancy predicted higher anxiety. Theoretically, this study may extend social norms research by identifying a possible boundary condition, where the effect of social-norm-based messages weakens when intended outcomes shift from visible behaviors to internal cognitive or emotional states, and by pointing to the potential role of perceived psychological distance as a receiver-centered contextual factor. Practically, the findings tentatively suggest that crisis communicators may benefit from tailoring social-norm-based messages to audiences' psychological distance, emphasizing emotional support for psychologically close audiences and collective efficacy for distant ones.

latest_articles.title: Catalyst for Change or Barrier to Health? A Meta-Analysis Synthesizing the Impact of Social Identity Threat in Health Messages
latest_articles.abstract: The use of social identity in health messaging is burgeoning, yet an open question remains as to whether appeals to one’s social identity can consistently promote health behavioral change. As an emerging field of inquiry, research on social identity threat in persuasive health messages remains fragmented. To address the inconsistent empirical findings, we conducted a meta-analysis to synthesize the existing research. Based on 18 independent studies from 12 articles (combined N = 4,436), the results indicated that, compared to non-threatening health messages, social identity-threatening health messages led to stronger perceived social identity threat (d = 0.231, p = .001), but yielded no significant effect on health behavioral intentions (d = −0.034, p = .541). Subsequent subgroup analyses revealed that threatening ascribed identities (e.g., race and gender) exerted a stronger impact than acquired identities (e.g., smoking and obesity). Furthermore, a significant and negative effect on health behavioral intentions emerged for non-stigmatized health topics, but the effect for stigmatized topics was nonsignificant. Our findings offer a nuanced account of social identity threat in health messages. Theoretically, perceived social identity threat merits operationalization as a standalone variable rather than a manipulation check criterion, which will enable future research to map out the boundary conditions of social identity-threatening health messages and unpack the mediating mechanisms underlying their persuasive impact. Practically, message designers should be mindful that identity-based appeals may backfire, particularly when addressing ascribed identities or non-stigmatized health topics.

latest_articles.title: TikTok News: How The Washington Post ’s Use of Platform Logics Affects Perceptions of Journalists and News Learning
latest_articles.abstract: In a period of high competition, many contemporary journalists attract audience attention by adopting the stylistic conventions (“logics”) of platforms like TikTok to deliver news online. However, the effects of this content on audience trust and learning remain unclear. Using two online experiments, we examine whether audiences perceive journalists as credible and learn from news videos employing TikTok logics, compared to traditional print articles. Results indicate that journalists using TikTok logics may effectively capture attention but are viewed as less trustworthy, credible, professional, and knowledgeable, though more likable, than print journalists. Learning outcomes are similar across formats.
affiliations: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA

latest_articles.title: When Epistemic Authority Collapses: Linking Fake News Media Perception and Conspiracy Beliefs to Disinformation Vulnerability
latest_articles.abstract: Citizens increasingly need to detect and filter disinformation, yet we know little about why some are more vulnerable than others. We examine whether forms of skepticism toward traditional epistemic authorities—fake news media perception (FNMP) and conspiracy beliefs—are associated with disinformation vulnerability. Using two-wave survey data from Spain ( N W1 = 1,207; n W2 = 821), we find that FNMP is widespread, not a fringe phenomenon. Conspiracy beliefs predict vulnerability across cross-sectional, lagged, and autoregressive models. Support for FNMP as a predictor is partial and not sustained in autoregressive models. Evidence for the interaction between FNMP and conspiracy beliefs is weak.

latest_articles.title: Does It Take Two to Benefit From Self‐Expansion? Dyadic Response Surface Analyses of Self‐Expansion and Relationship Satisfaction in Daily Life
latest_articles.abstract: Relational self‐expansion—the process of broadening one's self through novel and exciting experiences with a romantic partner—is important for relationship maintenance. Although theory and empirical research suggest that self‐expanding experiences enhance relationship satisfaction, it remains unclear whether partners need to experience similarly elevated levels of self‐expansion on a daily basis or similarly high levels of self‐expansion across time for these benefits to emerge. In four daily diary studies ( N = 512 couples), we assessed both partners' relational self‐expansion and relationship satisfaction across 21 consecutive days. Dyadic response surface analyses revealed no evidence that matching in daily fluctuations of self‐expansion or matching in heightened self‐expansion across time predicted greater relationship satisfaction. Instead, couples who reported higher self‐expansion reported higher satisfaction, and actor effects were consistently stronger than partner effects. Novel to this investigation, daily relationship satisfaction was lower only when self‐expansion was low, with moderate and high levels yielding similarly high satisfaction. These findings suggest that the overall level of self‐expansion of each partner's experiences, rather than similarity between partners, plays an essential role in sustaining relationship satisfaction.

latest_articles.title: Busy brains in the algorithm: TikTok’s platformed conditions for experiential gonzo expertise
latest_articles.abstract: This article explores how TikTok’s technological structures and features shape rhetorical invention and performances of health expertise. By illustrating how high-visibility ADHD-influencers can assemble authority through ethotic appeals and how their creative rhetorical performance is conditioned by TikTok, I develop the notion of experiential gonzo expertise to argue that a new kind of expertise is enabled and shaped by platform-specific affordances. Experiential gonzo expertise captures the rhetorical performance of an experience-based expertise that merges fact and fiction, in an environment with increased focus on the individual and declining trust in institutional expertise. The article highlights how agency emerges in the interplay between the content creators and the platform. By illustrating how TikTok shapes rhetorical performances through platform-specific affordances and exemplifying how the combined agency of TikTok and content creators constitute expertise in the rhetorical style of gonzo, the study’s findings inform broader health trends connected to human–machine interaction.

latest_articles.title: Human-in-the-Loop Pedagogy: Reframing Technical Communication Education in the Age of AI
latest_articles.abstract: Generative AI is becoming part of technical communication workflows, but programs still need a grounded way to teach students how to use it while preserving rhetorical judgment, editorial responsibility, and audience awareness. This article proposes a human-in-the-loop pedagogy that treats AI as a system whose outputs must be defined, guided, evaluated, and constrained by human writers. It offers a heuristic for integrating AI into writing instruction while reinforcing the field’s core competencies.

latest_articles.journal: Annals of the International Communication Association
latest_articles.title: Content escalation, content homogenization, and user immersion: a three-dimensional conceptualization of online rabbit holes
latest_articles.abstract: Online environments are often described as drawing users into a “rabbit hole.” While the term is frequently invoked in both academic and popular discourse, there is little consensus on what precisely constitutes an online rabbit hole. This lack of consensus has resulted in research on this phenomenon being conceptually fragmented and inconsistent. The current scoping review addresses this gap by systematically examining how online rabbit holes have been conceptualized and operationalized. Through a critical synthesis of 30 studies, we derive three recurring dimensions in the different conceptualizations of the online rabbit hole: content escalation, content homogenization, and user immersion. Building on these three key dimensions, we propose a comprehensive three-dimensional conceptual framework for understanding online rabbit holes and offer recommendations for accurately measuring and detecting them.
